chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from some of his companions from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

Indeed, the People of the Book and all those who have a covenant (dhimmah), if one of the spouses converts to Islam, they remain upon their marriage, and he is not permitted to take her out of the abode of Islam to another, nor should he spend the night with her, but rather he should come to her during the day.

As for the polytheists, such as the polytheists of the Arabs and others, they remain upon their marriage until the expiration of the waiting period (iddah). If the woman converts and then the man converts before the expiration of her waiting period, she is his wife. But if he does not convert until after the expiration of the waiting period, then she is divorced from him and there is no claim of him upon her.
And likewise all those who do not have a covenant. And it is not appropriate for the Muslim to marry a Jewish woman or a Christian woman while he finds a free woman or a slave woman.

Al-Shaykh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And the marriage of the Nāsibiyyah (female) who manifests enmity towards the Family of Muhammad (peace be upon them) is not valid, and there is no objection to the marriage of the weak/subjugated among them.

key_terms.أَهْلَ الْكِتَابِ: People of the Book (Jews and Christians)
key_terms.النَّاصِبِيَّةِ: Female Nāsibi (one who manifests enmity, specifically towards Ahl al-Bayt)

ai.seo_question: What happens to the marriage of a Muslim and a non-Muslim spouse when one converts to Islam?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi elaborates on this ruling by distinguishing between the People of the Book and polytheists, while notably extending the prohibition to 'Nasibiyyah' women who display enmity toward the Ahl al-Bayt, a key Shia jurisprudential criterion. The text clarifies that for those without a covenant, the marriage dissolves if the husband does not convert before the wife's iddah expires, emphasizing the temporal nature of the bond in mixed-faith scenarios. This reflects the Shia emphasis on both theological compatibility and political loyalty (walayah) in marital unions.
